paper_title: BridgeWAM: Bridging Video and Action Experts via Latent Bridge Queries

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space. Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Decoupling expert depths and reusing LBQs during action denoising yield a 5.06B model with a 30-layer Video Expert and a two-layer Action Expert, achieving 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating effective task execution and strong generalization with an ultralight action head. Ablations support joint representation adaptation and unified LBQ conditioning. Relative to Fast-WAM, BridgeWAM reduces single-sample inference FLOPs by 28.72% in simulation profiling and real-robot latency to 77.1 ms (a 2.47-fold speedup). Qualitative experimental results further indicate preferential attention to target objects and task destinations across perturbations.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: World Action Models (WAMs) aim to predict robot actions from visual observations, language instructions, and proprioceptive state while retaining the broad visual priors of video-generation models. Useful WAMs must therefore simultaneously predict precise action chunks, remain robust when scenes and objects change, and run with low enough latency for closed-loop control. Recent WAMs have improved these properties by coupling Video Expert and an Action Expert with Mixture-ofTransformers (MoT) attention Ye et al. (2026); Bi et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026b); Yuan et al. (2026). However, information transfer between the two modalities remains largely unchanged. WAM designs progressively simplify inference from joint videoaction generation to lighter visual conditioning. Joint models process current and future video, action, and state tokens together Ye et al. (2026). IDM-style models use asymmetric attention: the video branch operates independently while the action branch reads the visual sequence, but future-video generation remains necessary Li et al. (2026b); Zhang et al. (2026). Fast-WAM then removes future-video generation at inference to reduce latency, retaining MoTs direct video K/V interface to action attention Yuan et al. (2026). However, these layer-wise MoT designs retain central limitations. First, each Video Expert layer directly exposes its dense visual features to the corresponding action layer by concatenating video and action keys/values, making task-relevant information and redundant details compete for attention. Prior work has found that action generation may allocate excessive attention to task-irrelevant visual regions, interfering with the use of task-relevant information and impairing task execution Li et al. (2026a). Furthermore, reliance on task-irrelevant scene cues may weaken policy generalization under visual distribution shifts Sun et al. (2026). Second, one-to-one layer coupling forces both experts to have equal depth, introducing redundant parameters and inference overhead. Excessive action-side capacity may favor memorizing specific scene patterns over learning generalizable environmental regularities, weakening generalization. WAMs therefore need learnable interface that operates in compact latent space and enables the Action Expert to allocate more attention to taskrelevant visual features while allowing action supervision to shape visual representations. It should decouple expert depths, reducing redundant parameters and improving inference efficiency. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), new architecture that overcomes these limitations, and instantiate it as BRIDGEWAM, with an overview shown in Fig. 1. As illustrated in Fig. 2, BoE preserves modality-specific computation and connects the two experts through compact set of Latent Bridge Queries (LBQS), rather than directly mixing video and action tokens. Within the Video Expert, 32 LBQS aggregate the visual, language, and proprioceptive priors needed for action generation into shared, limited latent space, providing the Action Expert with latent features optimized for action generation through iterative learning. During end-to-end optimization, action-loss gradients flow through the LBQS into the Video Expert, guiding it to produce representations better suited to the Action Experts learning and prediction. BoE decouples the depths of the two experts. BRIDGEWAM combines 30-layer Video Expert with two-layer alternating crossself-attention Action Expert: cross-attention retrieves information from the LBQS, while self-attention coordinates the action chunk. By retaining the backbones representational capacity with lightweight action head, this design balances efficiency and performance. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce BoE, videoaction interface built on limited latent space. BoE uses 32 LBQS to construct limited latent space that aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors into unified latent representation tailored to the Action Expert. Joint video action optimization sends action gradients through the LBQS to shape action-relevant video representations and trains the Action Expert to prioritize task-relevant visual information. We develop BRIDGEWAM with decoupled expert depths to balance efficiency and performance. BRIDGEWAM pairs 30-layer Video Expert with two-layer alternating crossself-attention Action Expert for LBQ readout and action-chunk coordination. The lightweight action head and reusable LBQ interface reduce redundancy in parameters and the cost of inference, yielding 5.06B-parameter BRIDGEWAM that retains the video backbones representational capacity while balancing performance and efficiency. We demonstrate that BRIDGEWAM overcomes the above limitations of MoT through simulation and real-world task evaluations and precise ablation studies. Meanwhile, we conduct systematic ablations, action-conditioned visual-routing visualizations, and efficiency analyses to examine the effects of the LBQ interface and Action Expert depth on task performance, the ability to generalize, and the cost of computation. 2 Figure 2: Comparison of the BoE and MoT architectures. BoE uses Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) to transfer action-relevant visual features between experts. Unlike MoTs matched-depth coupling, BoE decouples expert depths, enabling BRIDGEWAM to use only two layers in the Action DiT while retaining the full Video Expert for learning rich representations of visual information.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Generalist VisionLanguageAction Policies. Generalist visionlanguageaction (VLA) policies map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions. RT-1 and RT-2 scale behavior cloning and visionlanguage pretraining for cross-task generalization (Brohan et al., 2023; Zitkovich et al., 2023). OpenVLA, π0, π0.5, and GR00T N1 extend generalist control using large pretrained backbones with autoregressive, diffusion, or flow-matching action decoders (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025). Despite their strong ability to generalize semantically, these action-centric models learn physical dynamics only implicitly from demonstrations annotated with robot actions. This limitation motivates the development of World Action Models, which explicitly model how visual scenes evolve over time. World Action Models and VideoAction Coupling. World Action Models (WAMs) jointly model visual dynamics and robot actions, providing dense supervision for scene evolution and physical interactions (Gao et al., 2026; Cen et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026). DreamZero jointly denoises future-video and action latents, enabling cross-modal interaction throughout inference (Ye et al., 2026). LingBot-VA and LingBot-VA 2.0 instead infer actions from predicted visual transitions through causal inverse dynamics (Li et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026). Fast-WAM reduces visual-imagination cost by training with future-video prediction but omitting future generation at inference, directly conditioning actions on latent Video DiT representations (Yuan et al., 2026). AHA-WAM further decouples their temporal roles through low-frequency video planner and high-frequency action executor (Cai et al., 2026). These WAMs primarily couple modalities through shared attention or by directly injecting dense video K/V representations. Cross-Modal Representation Transfer with Learnable Queries. MetaQuery uses learnable queries to extract generation conditions from frozen multimodal language model for transfer to diffusion model (Pan et al., 2025). GenCeption inserts learnable tokens into pretrained Video DiT to extract sparse structured predictions from its generative representations (Wang et al., 2026a). These studies establish compact, learnable query interfaces for task-relevant information extraction, primarily through one-way condition transfer or task readout. Building on this insight, our Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) use shared set of learnable queries to construct latent space for videoaction associations. Unlike MetaQuery, which extracts generation conditions from frozen multimodal language model, and GenCeption, which uses query tokens for sparse perception predictions, LBQs learn shared conditioning representations under joint video and action supervision, enabling the Video Experts representation learning and the Action Experts selective readout to adapt jointly. The Video Expert learns to write action-relevant physical representations into this shared latent space, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve from the same space the information required for control and action generation under changing physical conditions.

This fixed-size interface aligns visual, semantic, and proprioceptive information through joint video and action supervision without passing dense video tokens directly to the action branch during the conditioning and denoising processes. During training, LBQS read current-frame features and textstate context, while future-video queries read the LBQS to predict scene evolution. This design keeps action-conditioning information sources consistent across training and inference: LBQs are constructed from current observations, language instructions, and proprioceptive state, while future video provides training supervision without serving as an input to the bridge. Future-video generation can therefore be omitted at inference without changing how the Action Expert receives conditioning through LBQs. BoE therefore permits independent expert depths while keeping the interface compact: BRIDGEWAM combines 30-layer Video Expert with two-layer alternating crossself-attention Action Expert for compact action conditioning every denoising step.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: This section systematically evaluates BRIDGEWAM in terms of effective visual representation use and decoupled expert depths, examining the properties of BoE described in the Introduction. First, quantitative experiments in simulation and on real robots (Secs. 4.2 and 4.3) test whether an LBQ interface built on limited latent space and lightweight Action Expert can maintain effective task execution and generalize under environmental perturbations and distribution shifts. Meanwhile, ablation studies (Sec. 4.4) examine the joint adaptation of visual representations and action prediction, the aggregation of multimodal priors in limited latent space, and the effects of the Action Experts readout mechanism on task performance. Additionally, efficiency experiments (Sec. 4.4) compare parameter counts, computational cost, and inference latency across simulation-input profiling and real-robot deployment settings, testing whether decoupled expert depths and LBQ conditioning reuse translate into practical computational savings and, together with the quantitative results, assessing the balance between performance, generalization, and inference efficiency. Finally, qualitative analysis (Sec. 4.5) illustrates how BoE guides the Action Expert to assign greater attention to visual features of target objects and task destinations during action prediction, and examines the stability of this guidance under different perturbations.

sections.title: 4.3 QUANTITATIVE EVALUATION ON REAL ROBOTS
sections.content: Figure 4 compares task success and inference latency across the three methods. We deploy BRIDGEWAM on the PiPER from SongLing real-robot platform and evaluate four manipulation tasks with their OOD settings. We use task-specific staged scoring, with final scores computed over completed operation stages; for example, within single trial, successfully grasping an object and achieving the target each earn credit for their respective stages. For drink pick-and-place, grasping the drink, placing it within the target region, and leaving it upright each earn one point. Scoring criteria are detailed in Appendix A.4. These results show that the LBQ-mediated videoaction interface transfers beyond simulation and maintains stable, action-relevant representations under visual variation, observation noise, and execution disturbances during closed-loop manipulation.

sections.title: 4.4 ABLATION STUDIES AND EFFICIENCY
sections.content: We organize our ablations around four questions concerning joint visualaction adaptation, the readout of LBQs, multimodal conditioning, and the capacity of the Action Expert. We further compare videoaction coupling paradigms and inference efficiency. RQ1: Do video representations need to adapt jointly with action learning? We construct Frozen-Video-DiT variant that freezes the Video Expert from Fast-WAM trained on LIBERO and conditions the Action Expert through LBQs. In Table 4, this variant achieves average success rates of 85.50% on LIBERO and 25.48% on LIBERO-Plus, below the full models 98.25% and 72.24%, respectively. This result supports adapting video representations jointly with LBQ-conditioned action learning rather than directly relying on fixed, previously learned visual representations. sections.title: 4.5 QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS
sections.content: Action-Conditioned Visual Routing. To visualize which visual information is preferentially accessed by the Action Expert, we construct an action-conditioned visual-routing map. For BRIDGEWAM, we use the Action Experts attention scores over the latent bridge queries as query-importance weights and apply them to the corresponding LBQ-to-video-patch attention maps from the Video Expert. For Fast-WAM, we directly aggregate the action-to-visual-token attention across all Video-DiT layers. The resulting patch-space maps reveal the visual information preferentially routed toward action prediction; they should be interpreted as routing visualizations rather than strict causal attributions. Figure 5 shows representative routing maps for the two models under changes in background texture, lighting, camera viewpoint, robot initial state, object layout, and sensor noise. Experimental results show that the BoE not only enables the Action Expert to focus its attention on visual features that are more relevant to the current task, but also improves robustness to perturbations and enhances the models generalization performance across the evaluated visual changes. The layer selection follows each models visual-conditioning interface: Fast-WAM reads video features through layer-wise MoT connections, so we average attention across layers to summarize its overall attention preferences when accessing visual information at different depths; BRIDGEWAM conditions its Action Expert on the final LBQ representations, so we visualize the action-weighted LBQ-to-patch attention at this interface. These maps characterize architecture-specific routing preferences rather than provide matched-layer comparison.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BRIDGEWAM, to address two limitations of layer-wise MoT coupling: direct exposure of dense visual features to action layers and the requirement for matched expert depths. BoE uses compact, learnable LBQ interface to aggregate multimodal information, enabling selective retrieval by the Action Expert while allowing action supervision to shape video representations. Decoupling expert depths further enables lightweight action decoding without reducing the Video Experts depth. Together, these designs alleviate competition between task-relevant information and redundant visual details and reduce action-side computation, supporting favorable balance between task performance, generalization, and inference efficiency in the evaluated settings. 10 Limitations. During training on real-world robot tasks, however, we observed that this paradigm struggles to fit more complex, long-horizon manipulation tasks. BRIDGEWAM also retains instability observed in its Fast-WAM foundation. Future Outlook. Future work will focus on improving learning for long-horizon manipulation and constructing more stable, capacity-limited latent space. We will investigate how the bridge can preserve task-relevant information over longer temporal spans and provide more consistent conditioning for action prediction while maintaining the efficiency of lightweight action decoding.

sections.title: A ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: Code repository: https://github.com/jxfang04/BridgeWAM-code.git. This appendix records implementation and evaluation details that complement the main text. Unless stated otherwise, ablations use the same data splits, optimizer, numerical precision, denoising schedule, and checkpoint-selection rule of the full BRIDGEWAM model throughout these comparisons. A.1 EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN DETAILS In default training and inference, BRIDGEWAM combines pretrained backbone weights with randomly initialized task-specific modules. We detail the initialization of each component below. Pretrained visual and text components. The Video Expert uses the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B Video DiT, with 30 layers and hidden dimension of 3072. We load the corresponding pretrained weights for its attention and feed-forward networks (FFNs), text and timestep projections, and video output head. The VAE encoder and decoder also use pretrained Wan2.2 weights and remain frozen throughout training. The text conditioning is provided by UMT5-XXL. By default, the training process reads precomputed text embeddings without loading separate encoder for text; when enabled, the text encoder is initialized with its pretrained weights. Action Expert initialization. The Action Expert is two-layer Action DiT with hidden dimension of 1024, using an alternating crossself configuration that performs cross-attention followed by self-attention. Its two layers are initialized from the corresponding parameters of layers 0 and 29, respectively, in dimension-adapted, Wan-derived Action DiT checkpoint, including attention, FFN, and modulation parameters. The action timestep encoder (256 1024 1024), timestep modulation projection (1024 6144), and text projection (4096 1024 1024) are loaded from the same preprocessed checkpoint. The projection for action text is retained in the model but is not used in the forward pass under lbq only conditioning. Newly initialized projections. The action input encoder (7 1024), action output head (1024 7), two-layer LBQ-to-action projector (3072 1024 1024), and proprioceptive encoder (8 4096) use the default PyTorch Linear random initialization. Each linear layers weights and biases are sampled from uniform distribution whose bounds depend on that layers input dimension. Learnable embeddings and deterministic components. The action positional embeddings have shape [1024, 1024] and are initialized from zero-mean Gaussian distribution with standard deviation of 0.02. The first dimension specifies the maximum number of supported positions, rather than the executed action horizon. The 32 LBQs form learnable token bank of shape [1, 32, 3072], ini3072 0.01804. tialized from zero-mean Gaussian distribution with standard deviation of 1/ These embeddings are persistent trainable parameters and are not resampled at each forward pass. RoPE, attention masks, and the flow-matching scheduler are constructed from deterministic rules and configuration settings; they contain no trainable weights requiring random initialization. A.2 ABLATION PROTOCOL AND VARIANT DEFINITIONS We study action-head capacity, three interface ablations, and two alternative videoaction generation schemes. The interface and generation variants in Table 4 retain the default backbone and nominal two-layer Action Expert, with the specific changes described in the paragraphs below. Action-head depth. The depth study varies the Action Expert across 4, 8, 16, and 30 layers while keeping the Video Expert, LBQ count, training schedule, and evaluation protocol fixed. The 30-layer variant uses self-cross baseline action head whose nominal depth matches the Video Expert. Frozen-Video-DiT: adapting visual features for control. This variant tests whether the Video Expert must adapt its features to LBQ-mediated action learning. It retains the default training and inference architecture but initializes the Video DiT with Fast-WAM weights trained on LIBERO and freezes these weights. The Action Expert reads features produced by this frozen backbone through 15 the LBQs. Its LIBERO-Plus average drops to 25.48%, compared with 72.24% for the full model, supporting the need to adapt video representations jointly with action learning in this setting. MoT-readout: changing how actions read LBQs. This variant tests whether dedicated LBQ cross-attention improves the Action Experts use of task-relevant visual features. During training and inference, mixed self-attention concatenates LBQ and action keys/values, while action queries attend to textstate keys/values in cross-attention. The LIBERO-Plus average falls to 60.48%, indicating that this readout is less effective than the dedicated LBQ cross-attention used by the full model. Text-state-LBQ-input: mixing conditioning sources. This variant tests whether conditioning through unified LBQ space is preferable to providing the Action Expert with direct access to additional modalities. During training and inference, action queries in cross-attention read concatenated text, state, and LBQ keys/values. Its LIBERO-Plus average of 59.29% indicates reduced robustness to the evaluated perturbations relative to conditioning exclusively through LBQs in the full model. synchronous generation through LBQs. Joint: Joint propagates video, LBQ, and action states together in each denoising forward pass. At Video DiT layers 028, the same Action DiT layer-0 cross-attention block is repeatedly applied, reading the LBQs available at the start of each stage. Video queries attend to video and LBQ keys/values, whereas LBQ queries attend to video, LBQ, and action keys/values. At Video DiT layer 29, Action DiT layer 1 performs pure action self-attention once. Textstate conditioning enters only the Video/LBQ side. We stop gradients through the action keys/values read by LBQs, so the Action Expert is updated only by the action loss, while the Video Expert and LBQs receive both video and action supervision. At inference, video and action latents are denoised synchronously; the standard infer action() path returns actions without executing the VAE decoder. IDM: video generation followed by action generation. IDM first completes multi-step video denoising at inference, then conditions action generation on 32 LBQs representing the full video. After the action projector, these LBQs supply the sole keys/values for Action DiT layer-0 crossattention; layer 1 performs action-only self-attention. The same LBQ context is reused throughout the entire sequence of action denoising steps. Training instead uses two Video/LBQ forward passes: one predicts video and incurs the video loss; the other extracts action-conditioning LBQs from complete ground-truth video latents, which are either clean or noise-corrupted, with corruption probability of 0.5. Thus, training does not first sample complete video through iterative denoising. The current inference implementation also runs the VAE decoder. Table 8 distinguishes the three inference strategies. The 67.45% LIBERO-Plus result in Table 4 uses full-frame prefill at = 0 on the final video latent x0 to obtain the LBQs used as conditioning for action denoising. Table 8: IDM inference strategies. Together, these ablations support learning the external conditioning needed for the evaluated tasks within the Video Expert and consolidating it into fixed-size LBQ space for task-relevant action readout. The LIBERO efficiency results reported in Table 6 are measured for BRIDGEWAM, Fast-WAM, and Faster-WAM on NVIDIA H20Z GPUs in bfloat16, using an identical cached LIBERO input, an action horizon of 32, and 10 denoising steps. We average 10 measured inference calls after three warm-up calls. Timing begins immediately before Video DiT layer 0 and ends at the final clean action latent, excluding observation preprocessing, VAE encoding, text encoding, and postprocessing. Under this core-inference protocol, BRIDGEWAM takes 88.05 ms per call, compared with 405.91 ms for Fast-WAM, yielding 4.61 speedup. Runtime-shape FLOPs count linear and attention matrix multiplications and linear bias additions, with one multiplyadd counted as two FLOPs; action FLOPs include conditioning and all denoising steps. These FLOP counts explicitly exclude normalization, activations, RoPE, softmax, and other elementwise operations, including video K/V fusion. The Fast-WAM and BRIDGEWAM values are retained from earlier profiling runs. Faster-WAM was measured separately on an otherwise idle GPU, with CUDA-event latency of 321.16 ms; BRIDGEWAM achieves 3.65 speedup over Faster-WAM under this core-inference protocol. Its native one-pass future-cache configuration processes nine video frames, encoded as three latent frames with 294 video tokens, whereas the other two models process one observed latent frame with 98 video tokens. The cached observation and text inputs are identical across all three models. Faster-WAM uses 30 video and 30 action layers, with 2.745 video FLOPs and 0.476 action FLOPs (3.221 in total). Peak memory denotes per-process allocated GPU memory, including loaded parameters, in MiB (220 bytes), rather than the total amount of memory used on the device. Real-robot inference on NVIDIA RTX 5090. For the real-robot experiments on the PiPER from SongLing, we perform the models inference on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU. In this setting, BRIDGEWAM generates an action chunk in 77.1 ms, as also reported in Fig. 4.
